title: Ahaṁkāra: The Formation of “I” and “Mine”
reflection: Find the volume knob once today: notice when a remark is amplified by I, and turn it down a little.

questions.q: What are the three jobs of ahaṁkāra, according to Conversation 2.3?
o: Self-reference, appropriation and differentiation: a me at the centre, mine, and a boundary.
Memory, attention and judgement, which are the jobs of the other three workers of the mind.
Sensing, thinking and acting, which together make up the whole of a person’s day.
Pride, shame and fear, which are the three moods that the I-maker creates in us.
questions.e: Ahaṁkāra keeps a me at the centre of every scene, stamps experience mine, and draws the boundary between self and other.

questions.q: “Having an ego is a flaw, and the aim is to hate it and get rid of it.”
questions.e: Without a working I you could not take responsibility, keep relationships, learn or plan. In the Trika view the ego is infinite awareness in a narrowed, identified form. The aim is to see through it, not to hate it.
questions.c: The ego is necessary: see through it, do not hate it

questions.q: A man says, “I am this job,” and every comment on his work feels like an attack. What shift does Conversation 2.3 describe?
o: The functional I, I do this job, hardened into the absolute I, I am this job.
The functional I disappeared altogether, so that he no longer has any sense of himself left at all.
The absolute I softened a great deal, so that every remark now passes through him without any effect.
The job itself changed, so that the comments he receives now are different from the ones before it.
questions.e: The danger is one precise shift: when the functional I hardens into the absolute I, everything gets filtered through self-defence, attachment, fear, pride, shame and comparison.
questions.c: The danger is the functional I hardening into the absolute I

questions.q: What is the volume knob, in Conversation 2.3?
o: Ahaṁkāra amplifies experience as mine: you often cannot change the event, but you can lower the volume.
The size of the sound that the world makes, which a person can raise by speaking louder.
The strength of a memory, which fades by itself as long as a person leaves it alone.
The speed at which a person thinks, which can be turned up by practice and by effort.
questions.e: Two people get identical feedback. For I am my work, praise inflates and criticism wounds, the gain is high. For work is what I do, the same words are useful information, used and set down. This is a Module 2 modelling image.
questions.c: You often cannot change the event but you can lower the volume

questions.q: A teacher gets one critical comment among nine kind ones, and can think of nothing else. Which idea of Conversation 2.3 fits?
o: Loud ahaṁkāra steers manas to the one hurtful sentence among nine kind ones.
Weak memory, since she cannot recall the kind comments that she was given.
Poor judgement alone, since she has read the comment as worse than it was.
The Self, which has a taste for the hurtful, and so seeks out the criticism.
questions.e: Loud ahaṁkāra steers manas to the one hurtful sentence, tilts buddhi toward what did I do wrong, and hardens chitta into a self-story that recruits its own evidence.
questions.c: A loud I steers attention to the one hurtful sentence

questions.q: “‘I am worthless’ is as much ego as ‘I am superior,’ since both are an absolute self-image with the volume up.”
questions.e: The problem is never the size of the ego but the absoluteness of the identification. Self-criticism is not humility: it is the ego pointed inward. Real humility feels light.
questions.c: Both are ego: the problem is absoluteness, not size

questions.q: A woman is hard on herself and calls it humility. What does Conversation 2.3 suggest?
o: Harsh self-criticism is ego pointed inward; real humility feels light.
Harsh self-criticism is the best sign of humility, so she should continue with it.
Harsh self-criticism is a sign of strength, so she should not try to change it at all.
Harsh self-criticism is the Self speaking, so she should listen to what it says.
questions.e: Self-criticism is not humility. Both big ego and small ego are the same machine, an absolute self-image with the volume up.

questions.q: A man is told good news that contradicts his self-image, and he does not take it in. Why does Conversation 2.3 say insight alone rarely heals this?
o: The self-image filters out contradicting news, so the defences must soften by being seen.
The news was false, and so the self-image was right to refuse it when it came.
The man was not listening, so he must be asked again until he takes it in.
The insight was too small, so a larger one is needed to overcome the image.
questions.e: Loud ahaṁkāra even filters out good news that contradicts the self-image, which is why insight alone rarely heals. The defences must gently soften by being seen.
questions.c: Defences soften by being seen, not by argument

questions.q: What does Conversation 2.3 say about science and the sense of I?
o: The self is described as a process the brain builds, a self-model; identity threats act like bodily ones.
The self is a fixed thing in the brain, which can be found by looking in just the right place for it.
The self is an error, and science has shown that nothing at all stands behind it in any person.
The self is the same in every single person, and science finds no difference at all between them.
questions.e: Ego trouble appears in both directions, arrogance and fragile, shame-based collapse. Lab and contemplation converge: the everyday I is assembled, useful, and not the final truth of you.
questions.c: The I is assembled and useful, not the final truth

questions.q: A father notices that praise puffs him up and criticism flattens him. Which step fits Conversation 2.3?
o: Find the volume knob: notice the amplification, and turn the same words into information.
Avoid all feedback, so that nothing is ever able to move the volume in either way.
Raise the volume of praise, since it is the one thing that makes him feel strong.
Treat the criticism as the truth, since the pain of it shows how right it must be.
questions.e: You usually cannot change the event, but you can lower the volume, which is often far more effective than rearranging the world.
questions.c: Find the volume knob and turn it down
